guardrail_rejections.title: Nvidia live updates: Trump calls Huang saga a 'horrible thing' and 'so sad to see'
guardrail_rejections.content: This is CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down as CEO of the chipmaker he co-founded 33 years ago and built into a $4 trillion company that powered the artificial intelligence boom, the company announced Thursday. CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO. "The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," said board chair Harvey Jones in a release announcing the news. The company will begin the search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang and will consider both internal and external candidates, according to the release. Kress also provided a statement in the release, but Huang was not quoted. After a meteoric rise to fame due to Nvidia's central role in AI, Huang's dramatic fall has been even more rapid, following a series of stinging revelations about his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy. Huang, 63, apologized on Sunday for being "unfaithful to my wife," though he provided no details about the affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, who has worked for a Chinese company and Nvidia customer called Megaspeed. Late Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia CEO also had a separate affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at the chipmaker. Later that afternoon, The Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia's board met to discuss the company's future. Huang's downfall also puts the spotlight on President Donald Trump , who formed a particularly close relationship with the CEO of what, until recently, was the world's most valuable company. Huang became a key voice on U.S. AI policy while pushing for issues that were in Nvidia's interest, such as preserving access to open-source AI, and lobbying to allow chip exports to China. A flash poll of members of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council and Financial Advisor 100 on Thursday showed 18 respondents are planning to hold their Nvidia allocations steady in client portfolios. — Sharon Epperson President Trump called Huang on Tuesday, urging him to fight to keep his job as Nvidia CEO, The New York Times reported. The call was made after Huang publicly apologized for being unfaithful to his wife as reports were surfacing that he'd had an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Read The New York Times report here. —Lora Kolodny Hyphen Capital founder Dave Lu, whose non-profit fights discrimination against Asian-Americans, told CNBC that the Asian-American community has been "heartbroken" by news about Jensen Huang this week. Lu wrote, in an e-mail, "It's hard to describe what it meant to see someone who looked like us ascend to become the face of the AI revolution on the global stage. He was the immigrant rags to riches archetype of the American dream. From washing dishes at a Denny's to running the most valuable company in the world. Our kids were proudly dressing up in leather jackets for Halloween. That all came crashing down in a matter of days." One of Huang's reported paramours, Megaspeed businesswoman Alice Huang, was accused of being a Chinese spy, the investor said, but the U.S. government has not presented proof of espionage. "The use of these 'Red Scare' tactics is not new. But it's disheartening every time it happens, because it perpetuates the narrative that Asian-Americans are not to be trusted and are disloyal to our country. It also hurts Asian-American women, who have historically been hyper-sexualized by American media and are now being portrayed as honeypots and spies across the internet in memes." Lu also said Huang is being treated differently than white executives including Larry Ellison, Elon Musk, Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos, who all reportedly had extramarital affairs, or affairs with their subordinates in the case of Musk and Ellison, but kept their jobs. — Lora Kolodny Banking Committee Chairman Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) has called for Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3rd and December 10th, respectively. In a post on social network X, Scott wrote , "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology. I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee. The American people deserve answers." In a letter addressed to Huang, Sen. Scott warned the embattled Nvidia founder, "Should you fail to appear before the Committee on a voluntary basis, the Committee is prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas, to conduct this legitimate and necessary oversight." — Lora Kolodny Nvidia shares dropped Thursday after Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO. But investors who hold popular mutual funds and exchange-traded funds can largely shrug off volatility in the chipmaker's stock , according to financial advisors. "It's not a big deal," said Philip Chao, a certified financial planner and chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth. "Most people are just reacting to the sensational aspect of this [news]." For example, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ( VOO ), a roughly $1.7 trillion fund, had a stake of about 8.4% in Nvidia as of Sept. 30, according to most recent Vanguard data. With such a weighting, a 5% decline in Nvidia's stock would lead the fund to lose just 0.42% of its value, all else equal, according to an analysis by Experiential Wealth. A 10% decline would lead the fund to drop by 0.84%, according to the analysis. Of course, other stocks in the AI ecosystem could also fall. That might pull fund returns down further, at least in the short term, though such an outcome isn't a foregone conclusion, advisors said. — Greg Iacurci Jensen Huang's scandal is rippling through the markets — including China's underground trade of Nvidia chips. "This year the controls have already been extremely strict," one trader, who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the business, told CNBC. "They will likely get even stricter." The person said those in China trafficking the advanced American chips sought by Chinese AI companies were told to pause work into next week because of the drama engulfing the now former Nvidia CEO due to his extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. It's unclear how extensive the underground Nvidia chip trade is in China Shares of Chinese AI companies slid on Thursday on worries the U.S. would squeeze China's access to Nvidia chips. Alibaba shares shed around 7% in Hong Kong on reports that the Chinese tech giant was a customer of Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that had allegedly offered access to Nvidia chips under the management of Huang's alleged mistress. Alibaba didn't provide a comment. Another reason for the work stoppage, the person said, was the expectation of greater U.S. scrutiny due to President Donald Trump's arrival in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leadership meeting on Nov. 18. Shenzhen is a hub of Nvidia chip trafficking. Traders on Chinese social media offer advanced H200 chips, which are permitted by the Trump administration, for sale in China, as well as the still-banned cutting-edge Blackwell B300. They advertise that their stock is already in port cities such as Shenzhen and Shanghai. The current black market price of a set of eight B300 graphics processing units, or GPUs, for a server fetches 20 million yuan ($2.99 million), which is up five times from May and is nearly six times higher than the official U.S. price of $550,000, according to listings. — Eunice Yoon Shares of Nvidia declined 4.3% Thursday, hitting a new 52-week low early in the day, but significantly paring losses by the close. For much of the trading session Nvidia was on track to close below $4 trillion in market cap for the first time since July 2025, but the stock rose just above the benchmark heading into the close. — Caleigh Keating President Trump lamented the "horrible thing" that happened to Huang in an interview conducted hours after his close corporate ally resigned as Nvidia's CEO. Trump referenced Huang after telling conservative commentator Hugh Hewitt that the U.S. would be in "bad shape" if it lost its edge in artificial intelligence. "I've seen it. I study it. I'm genetically blessed. I have an uncle that was probably considered the number one professor in the history of MIT for 51 years," Trump said. "He was there, and he got the science award, the same award that I gave to Elon [Musk], and you know, I gave them out last week. We gave it to Google. We gave it to a lot of great people ... we gave it to Jensen," he said. "Frankly, that was a little before. But what a horrible thing that is! That's so sad to see that happen," Trump said. "But my uncle got the same award from Ronald Reagan. They presented it to me when when I was there last week, and it was sort of something. So I do have, I think, an inclination. I'm a believer in that, you know." — Kevin Breuninger The woman at the center of Jensen Huang's spy-sex scandal may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Huawei, Nvidia's biggest competitor in Beijing, according to findings from private intelligence firm Tesari shared exclusively with CNBC . Alice Huang was described as a top executive at Singaporean tech company Megaspeed in initial reporting from The New York Times revealing U.S. officials had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Jensen Huang on Sunday copped to an extramarital affair with an unnamed woman, following numerous additional reports about his close relationship with Alice Huang. The connections uncovered by Tesari may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the ousted Nvidia chief , and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Click here to read the full report. — Eamon Javers and Kevin Breuninger Two of Huang's kids, Madison and Spencer Huang, work at Nvidia. So does Madison's husband, Nico Caprez. Caprez has risen quickly through the ranks, becoming vice president of global AI infrastructure in January, after joining Nvidia as a corporate development manager in 2024. He was previously an alpine skier and consultant with Boston Consulting Group, and met the CEO's daughter in business school. Madison joined Nvidia as an intern in 2020 after training as a professional chef, then obtaining a Masters of Business Administration from the London Business school. She serves as a senior director of product marketing for the company's robotics division. Spencer also works in robotics, serving as the director of product management. He joined Nvidia in 2022 as a product manager in the company's Isaac Sim Cloud division after obtaining an undergraduate degree from Columbia College Chicago and an MBA from New York University's Stern School of Business. In an all-hands meeting last year, Jensen Huang was asked by employees about nepotism. In a recording of this meeting heard by CNBC, he said that hiring children of Nvidia employees "is a good idea if it's done properly, if it's done on merits." He said he was proud of his kids, and added that children of Nvidia executives working at the company were "even better than their parents." — Lora Kolodny and Isabel O'Brien Huang had an "intimate relationship" with a second Nvidia employee, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. A day earlier, The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care. Huang on Sunday admitted to one affair following reports of his intimacy with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, reportedly believed by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Reuters is not naming the second employee. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. — Kevin Breuninger Jensen Huang's rise, becoming a "monarch" that was essentially "co-branded so that you can't separate" the CEO from the company, was a corporate governance problem, according to Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management. "There are a lot of times [corporate boards] are beholden," Sonnenfeld told CNBC's Morgan Brennan on "Morning Call." "They're smitten by the CEO; kind of idolatry." Nvidia's board reflects that. Prior to his exit on Thursday, Huang was one of 11 members of the board, which had no chair. None of Nvidia's 10 other board members are current or former S&P 500 CEOs. On average, they've been on the board for 15 years. Across the S&P 500, the average tenure of an independent director is 7.8 years and roughly one in every four directors is a former CEO, according to 2025 data from the Conference Board . Sonnenfeld said "no one was equipped to step in." "Somebody needs to ask some questions, and that's what's missing here," he said. — Ian Thomas Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan, Vice Chair of the House Financial Services Committee and a Republican, said it would be "helpful" if Commerce Department Secretary Howard Lutnick testified to Congress in public, in the wake of reports that he stalled a crackdown of firms routing Nvidia chips to China by President Donald Trump . "They have not been as cooperative as they should be. They have not been as transparent with Congress, much less I think others within that system," Huizenga said of the Commerce Department Thursday. "I want to hear from them a commitment and a recommitment to national security and making sure that these very important technologies and pieces of equipment and chips and other things aren't falling into the wrong hands." Huizenga told CNBC the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of Commerce that handles export controls, needs to take Congressional concerns about the export of Nvidia chips to China seriously. "The notion of being able to slow this down and be more selective is actually a positive thing, and what I mean by [that is] not slowing down the technology, but slowing down that transfer of technology," he said. The Financial Services Vice Chair said he didn't expect to hear much from ousted CEO Jensen Huang on chip policy besides what he's said publicly, but that he finds Huang's jeopardization of national security "disappointing" and "disturbing." — Caleigh Keating, Laura Garrison Huang's supporters are mourning his departure from the company — literally, it appears. Photographs show several bouquets of flowers, and at least one candle, have been placed at Nvidia's sign outside its corporate office in Santa Clara, California. — Kevin Breuninger Huang's resignation is the latest setback for Silicon Valley billionaires who bet big on Trump. Few tech executives enjoyed as much access to Trump as Huang, who successfully pushed the administration to ease restrictions on chip sales to China. Nvidia committed at least $26 million to Trump-backed projects, including the White House ballroom , and spent a record $2.15 million on federal lobbying in the third quarter. His departure comes just over a week after Republicans suffered sweeping midterm losses despite massive spending by the industry's wealthiest figures, including a record $474 million from Elon Musk . The elections also exposed growing public opposition to the AI buildout , a backlash Democrats are poised to tap into as they take control of Congress. — Luke Fountain Huang has hired the law firm Paul Weiss, CNBC confirmed. It's not immediately clear what he will use its services for. The New York Times was first to report the development. —Ashley Capoot Jensen Huang's ouster threatens to put the U.S. at a competitive disadvantage in the global AI race, according to CJ Muse, a semiconductor analyst at Cantor Fitzgerald. "We are giving up the lead in AI in my view to China," Muse told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "Jensen was the most optimistic supporter of AI, obviously created the foundational technology that is enabling frontier models and for the U.S. to be a leader in AI." He added, "I think that him being forced out is a major loss for Nvidia and also a major loss for the United States." There were likely Nvidia shareholders who wanted Huang to "stay and fight," but uncertainty around the outcome of an internal investigation into Huang's conduct, as well as the specter of congressional probes, made it "incredibly difficult" for the board to retain Huang, Muse said. "On a positive note, there are very talented people at Nvidia," Muse said. "On the other hand, Jensen is a one of a kind founder. I think you can count on your hand the number of people that can build a business like him, and so the key will be how do they maintain their technological roadmap over the coming five years." Muse on Thursday cut his price target on Nvidia stock from $350 to $250, while maintaining his overweight rating. — Annie Palmer Nvidia's board decided last night to oust longtime CEO Jensen Huang, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said sentiment quickly turned after the report of a second alleged affair. The team worked late into the night on its communications strategy and made an official decision this morning, before naming Kress as interim CEO, the person added. — Seema Mody, Samantha Subin Super Micro Computer shares fell 12% after Semafor reported that the U.S. Justice Department is looking into whether organizations associated with Alice Huang, the woman suspected to be a Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia's Jensen Huang, were involved in diverting Super Micro's artificial intelligence hardware to China. In March, U.S. prosecutors charged three people who had been connected with Super Micro, including co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw, with smuggling billions worth of Nvidia-powered servers into China. Liaw and the other two are no longer affiliated with the company, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Liaw's attorney declined to comment. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York, which originally made the allegations about the smuggling, is leading the investigation, according to Semafor , which cited two officials. — Jordan Novet University of Colorado Law professor Ann Lipton, a corporate law and governance expert, said that following Huang's resignation, the Nvidia board will need to "move swiftly" to present a succession plan, which will be difficult given Huang's centrality to the business. The board should also "make clear to investors that it is on top of the situation" and how it is filling holes left in Huang's absence. The CEO's resignation, Lipton said in an e-mail, "demonstrates the seriousness of the underlying allegations, and will strengthen any shareholder claims regarding damages, the importance of any misrepresentations, and Huang's likely knowledge of the truth. " Following reports that Huang had an affair with a purported Chinese spy, Rosen Law Firm in New York filed a proposed class action lawsuit on behalf of investors who saw the value of their Nvidia stock decline rapidly. Rosen Law attorney Phillip Kim told CNBC in an e-mail that investor interest in joining the class action has been high. "It's a widely held stock," he wrote. In just a few days, he added, "several hundreds of investors" had contacted his firm, ranging "from mom and pops to investors with very large losses." — Lora Kolodny Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top-ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Trump's reported reaction to troubling U.S. intelligence about Huang demands scrutiny. "All the reports say that Trump knew what took place and just basically made it like it was no big deal," Meeks said when asked if Trump was too trusting of Huang, his close ally. "Those are the things that have to be looked at," Meeks said. When asked if Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick or Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler should be called to testify, Meeks said, "Look, I think that anybody that could answer some questions, anybody that might have been involved." "If it's up to me, I'm going to at least have some questions or some hearings. The American people need to know," he added. — Kevin Breuninger and Justin Papp Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said Huang's departure does not obviate the need for him and Nvidia to answer to Congress. "Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer wrote in an X post. "The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset," Schumer wrote. "Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump's relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One? Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships," the Senate leader wrote. — Kevin Breuninger Democratic leaders on the Senate Finance Committee and House Ways and Means Committee are launching an investigation into the Trump administration's approval for the export of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to Chinese government-linked companies. Their letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announcing the probe was sent by Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Rep. Richard Neal, D-Mass., the respective ranking members of the Senate and House committees. Wyden and Neal noted that, despite Trump's reported knowledge of U.S. intelligence showing Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy, his administration "did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat." "On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang's compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales," the letter read. They described a "scheme" in which Trump would let Nvidia sell Taiwanese H200 chips to Chinese companies, provided they undergo a security review in the U.S. and receive an export license, subjecting them to 25% U.S. tariffs. "The Trump Administration's ostensible attempt to mask an unconstitutional export tax as a national security tariff action — benefitting both Nvidia and the Chinese government — raises serious concerns within our Committees' jurisdiction over matters relating to taxation and tariffs," they wrote. — Kevin Breuninger Jensen Huang's $140 billion Nvidia stake is largely held by trusts that are co-owned with his wife, Lori, according to SEC filings. The arrangement further complicates Huang's sudden exit from the company, but could prove to be a stabilizing force for the shares, since the trusts make it more difficult for either Huang or his wife to quickly sell, lawyers told CNBC. Here is why ultra-rich founders use these trusts and how they could work in the event of a divorce. — Hayley Cuccinello Employees inside Nvidia are struggling to come to grips with long-tenured CEO Jensen Huang's departure, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. But the mood at the company is "more complicated" than the headlines depict, according to the person, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The person described employees in tears, noting that many had come to idolize Huang and regard him as integral to Nvidia's identity. The person also sensed a "more nervous energy" around leadership and expressed concerns that the noise around Huang's affairs could impact execution. The board, they said, is in a difficult position, figuring out how to protect Huang and the company, while also ensuring it doesn't drag down the business. — Samantha Subin, Spriha Srivastava Beyond its impact on Nvidia, Huang's departure has deep ramifications for the AI industry that has turned him into a global spokesperson and celebrity, traversing the globe in his trademark leather jacket, touting the power of advanced chips, models and agents. Huang has seeded the market with numerous companies that buy Nvidia GPUs, building his company's influence and establishing a deep roster of customers, beyond the hyperscalers. Nvidia has used its balance sheet to backstop leases and chip sales, and has become the centerpiece of the industry, acting as technology supplier, customer, investor, financier and partner to scores of AI companies. "He's Mr. AI. He speaks for the industry," said Jeff Christian, CEO of Christian and Timbers, an executive search firm. "He's connected financially to everybody either through partnerships, or through lending the money to buy chips." — Kif Leswing Nvidia's growing credit support mechanisms for its customers, often offered in the form of a backstop on a loan or other type of debt facility, have come under question in recent months as the chipmaker's exposure has ballooned. According to its last quarterly financial filing in July, Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet backstops for neoclouds, as well as $20 billion dedicated to leases it had signed with the intention of renting out data center capacity. That's all in addition to the whopping $105 backstop deal Nvidia offered OpenAI to rent SB Energy's planned Ohio mega data center campus in August . In recent months, Nvidia's standards for its partners to require a backstop have become more stringent. The Information reported that CFO Colette Kress was against the $105 billion OpenAI deal, for example. Adil Malik, a partner at Origin Partners, a digital infrastructure-focused M&A advisory firm, says he noticed a change in the standards Nvidia needed to support a backstop for his clients around three months ago. "The offtake language before, maybe a non-binding LOI [letter of intent] from an offtaker would be enough, and it didn't have to be a very well known one that's an established company or AAA rated," he said, stating that now, a letter of intent "is usually not good enough. There has to be some level of offtake commitment, whether it's a binding LOI or ideally an executed offtake contract. Binding LOIs have been even extremely difficult now." — Isabel O'Brien Nvidia's fortunes exploded after OpenAI released ChatGPT in late 2022, leading to soaring demand for the chipmaker's graphics processing units, or GPUs. Nvidia's stock is up about 14-fold since then, even with a recent pullback related to the Huang scandal and the broader sell-off in the AI trade. — Kif Leswing House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Democrats are investigating the Huang spy scandal as they prepare to take over majority control of the House and Senate. The incoming Democratic chairs of the House intelligence and foreign affairs committees "are leading the effort to get to the bottom of what has happened," said Jeffries, who is poised to be House speaker in the next Congress. "There certainly are more questions than answers," Jeffries said at a press conference on Capitol Hill. "We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation," Jeffries added. "And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens." Asked by CNBC for his reaction to Huang's resignation, Jeffries said it "was the right thing to do." "Now we have to get to the bottom of whether America's national security has been compromised," Jeffries said. — Kevin Breuninger and Irit Skulnik Analysts are growing bearish on Nvidia after an espionage scandal led to the exit of the company's CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang. Several shops on the Street downgraded the artificial intelligence infrastructure stock, citing the leadership questions that are swirling around Nvidia in the wake of the scandal. "We find it hard to advocate stepping in here in size as there will no doubt be more allegations to come (there is a trope that says if you find two ants in your kitchen the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two...), both from internal issues as well as headlines related to the business, new governmental investigations etc.," Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said Thursday in a note to clients. Keybanc analyst John Vinh echoed that sentiment in his own note to clients. "We believe Huang's departure represents a material increase in strategic, organizational, and execution risk that warrants a higher risk premium and lower valuation multiple for the stock," Vinh wrote. "While we expect core fundamentals to remain strong for the foreseeable future, we believe it will be challenging for NVDA to find a successor with the same leadership and strategic vision as Huang." — Liz Napolitano Huang had emerged as one of Trump's closest allies in the AI build-out. In May, Huang joined Trump on a trip to China, and in August, while on stage at the All-In Summit to discuss AI safety and regulation, he took a call from Trump and put him on speakerphone. "I'm with you all the way," Trump told Huang and the audience. With Democrats poised to take over both houses of Congress and promising to investigate various matters related to Nvidia, Huang's status in Washington, D.C., was poised to change dramatically even before the affairs became public. — Kif Leswing Interim CEO Colette Kress will gather the company's executive team today at the chipmaker's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. Kress will discuss leadership and continuity plans with the group of high-level executives, according to the person, who asked not to be named because the details are confidential. — Seema Mody, Annie Palmer House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla. told reporters on Thursday that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will testify before Congress ahead of Thanksgiving. "He has agreed to come," Mast said. "We're in negotiations for which day." The hearing will likely be under oath and transcribed, with multiple committees involved. Mast said he told Huang that he would "subpoena him" if necessary. Mast said Congress isn't ruling out "public hearings for other people or other things down road." — Samantha Subin Retail traders rushed in to buy Nvidia shares following Jensen Huang's resignation, with the stock drawing the biggest opening bid from individual traders ever recorded by Vanda Research. In the first 30 minutes of the regular session, retail traders bought a net $111 million of Nvidia shares, more than 40x a normal open. The buying on Thursday follows multiple days of strong retail demand for the chipmaker's stock. It was the most heavily bought security across Vanda's universe Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday this week, commanding multiple times more net buying than the next most-bought security. NVDA has accounted for 61% of all retail net buying this week. Demand has also spilled over into leveraged products: Retail investors put $42.5 million into six 2x long Nvidia ETFs from Monday through Wednesday, one of the largest three-day inflows on record, Vanda said. — Nick Wells Jensen Huang denied allegations that he had compromised national security or Nvidia secrets after reports of the Alice Huang affair. The news sparked concerns that Nvidia knew companies based in Singapore and Malaysia had been evading U.S. export controls in accessing its technology. The board said on Tuesday that it had hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate the intelligence allegations. — Kif Leswing Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., said he expects Congress to conduct oversight of the Jensen Huang affair even after the embattled tech CEO's resignation. "In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Thune said when asked by reporters if there would be congressional investigations into the matter. Thune earlier this week was reelected Senate Republican leader. The GOP will be in the minority come January, after Democrats won at least 55 seats in the upper chamber. — Garrett Downs Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue lamented Huang's ouster from Nvidia, writing in a LinkedIn post that it's "a really sad day." Nvidia in September agreed to acquire Hugging Face, a leading platform for open-source AI models, in a deal worth about $12.9 billion . The company expects the deal to close in the first half of 2027. "This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened," Delangue wrote. "It's a really sad day!" He continued, "But I want to make one thing clear: we'll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let's go!" The Hugging Face deal, which is the second-largest in Nvidia's history, has attracted scrutiny from regulators. CNBC previously reported that the U.S. Department of Justice is probing the acquisition and how it could impact competition in the AI market. — Annie Palmer House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told reporters on Thursday that he still has confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick despite reporting this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China . Mast also said he wanted Congress to investigate the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal. The New York Times reported earlier this week that the company's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to commerce investigators looking into Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The commerce investigation into Huang's company, Megaspeed, was then transferred to the Justice Department. "The people that we deal with in BIS, those are the ones that are at the granular level of dealing with Nvidia and chips," Mast said. Mast said he hadn't spoken to Lutnick or Kessler since the revelations. — Justin Papp Creative Strategies CEO Ben Bajarin called Huang a "trendsetter" and said his exit creates "a huge shakeup and an impact to the industry." "Anytime ... you lose a founder-level-type of charisma who really has been looked upon as the, this trendsetter for the industry, the spokesperson for this moment that we have in this technology build out, that's going to be a loss," Bajarin told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Thursday. Uncertainty over who will ultimately take the helm at Nvidia only adds to the challenge, according to the Creative Strategies CEO. Bajarin sees VP of Nvidia's data center business Ian Buck as the most logical candidate to be Huang's permanent replacement, with an internal pick likely preferable to an external candidate. "You have to have deep semiconductor expertise ... it's a very short list of people who can do that at this scale." "What they need to bring back is somebody who can normalize things and be that type of person who can keep the troops aligned, keep them convicted on what they're doing in their engineering, and preserve that culture," Bajarin said. — Caleigh Keating Nvidia could face sustained selling pressure as investors reassess the value of Jensen Huang's leadership, according to Michael Landsberg, chief investment officer at Landsberg Bennett Private Wealth Management. Landsberg described Huang's resignation as the worst-case scenario. While he called CFO Colette Kress highly capable and respected, he questioned how the innovation of Nvidia will evolve without Jensen. "Part of the value proposition of this stock was not just its chips, but Jensen's vision and ability to steer the company," Landsberg said. "The stock is now pricing in a leadership discount, as the Jensen premium evaporates," he said, adding that while it is possible for Nvidia to navigate this storm, it's likely going to take time.
